title: Q&A with Climate Scientist David Victor, Part 3: The Future of Energy | Dimensional
gist: David Victor (UC San Diego/Brookings) argues CCS is an old technology held back mainly by unreliable policy, with Norway's Northern Lights a key proof point but scale decades away and unattractive to private investors for now. On nuclear, rising data-center-driven demand favors existing and restarted US reactors, SMRs offer factory-built cost potential, and Korea/China's repeatable builds beat the West's bespoke, overrun-prone projects.

insights.claim: Carbon capture's core technology (acid gas scrubbing) dates to a 1930s patent, so the bottleneck for CCS is not invention but policy, cost control and systems integration.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: CCS investment risk is policy and execution risk, not technology-discovery risk.
insights.quote: The patent on acid gas scrubbing—which is the main technology used to capture CO2—goes back to the 1930s.
insights.locator: What I find interesting about carbon

insights.claim: Per David Victor, almost all carbon capture projects over the past 20-25 years failed, most often because of insufficient reliable policy support rather than technology costs or integration issues.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Subsidy/regulatory durability is the key diligence variable for any CCS exposure.
insights.quote: but more often there wasn’t enough reliable policy support
insights.locator: The idea of capturing CO2 and putting

themes.theme: Northern Lights as CCS proof point

insights.claim: Norway's Northern Lights project (a TotalEnergies-Equinor-Shell JV backed by the Norwegian government and EU, operational since 2024) ships CO2 by sea to a hub and pipes it to a reservoir 2,600 meters under the seabed, and David Victor calls it the most interesting CCS project in the world.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Track Northern Lights cost and reliability disclosures as the benchmark for CCS economics.
insights.quote: The Northern Lights project in Norway, which has been operational since 2024, is the most interesting carbon capture project in the world right now.
insights.locator: The Northern Lights project in Norway

insights.claim: Northern Lights demonstrates that CCS can be applied to concentrated industrial CO2 sources such as natural gas processing, cement and steel plants, not just power plants, and some capture technologies can be retrofitted onto existing plants.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Addressable market for CCS extends to hard-to-abate heavy industry and the existing asset base.
insights.quote: some of the carbon capture technologies can be retrofitted on existing plants

insights.claim: The shared transport-and-storage hub model (multiple capture sites shipping CO2 to one storage site) lets emitters decarbonize without building their own sequestration, though it remains a very expensive first-of-a-kind project.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Hub-and-spoke CO2 infrastructure is a likely template for future CCS build-outs.
insights.quote: It is a very expensive, first-of-a-kind project.

insights.claim: For carbon capture to matter for climate at scale, tens of thousands of plants would need to adopt it, and scaling such an industrial system requires a couple of decades of operating experience.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Material CCS impact is a 2040s+ story; near-term volumes will be small.
insights.quote: To be relevant at scale, tens of thousands of plants would have to use carbon capture and sequestration.
insights.locator: Victor: To be relevant at scale

insights.claim: Few if any private investors will finance CCS at scale until early projects prove reliability and cost declines, because investors want boring projects with predictable returns rather than scientifically exciting but financially scary ones.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Expect CCS to remain dependent on state and major-oil balance sheets for a decade or more.
insights.quote: Most investors want boring projects that yield predictable returns, not projects that are exciting to scientists but laden with scary financial prospects.
insights.locator: Until that happens, few if any

insights.claim: Early backers of first-of-a-kind CCS projects are effectively buying the option for rapid scaling a decade or two later as learning curves bring costs down.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: First-mover sponsors may capture know-how and cost advantages if CCS scales.
insights.quote: The backers of these early projects are creating the possibility of more rapid scaling a decade or two down the road

insights.claim: Despite the long timeline, David Victor is optimistic that carbon capture and sequestration can slow the rate of global temperature increases.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Long-dated policy support for CCS is plausible given expert optimism.
insights.locator: Even though it may take some time

themes.theme: Nuclear revival driven by demand growth

insights.claim: The nuclear opportunity favors existing plants over new builds: existing reactors become more valuable for power-hungry clean-energy buyers, while new plants remain costly and risky.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Prefer owners of operating nuclear fleets over new-build developers.
insights.quote: existing nuclear plants become more interesting, while new nuclear plants can still be very costly and risky
insights.locator: Victor: For a company—or a country

insights.claim: Unlike the early-2000s nuclear revival, when US and European power demand was flat or declining, power demand is now rising due to data centers, electrification and to some degree EVs, making the US the most interesting nuclear market.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Demand-side growth makes this nuclear cycle structurally stronger than the 2000s 'renaissance'.
insights.quote: When there was renewed interest in nuclear energy in the early 2000s, power demand in the US and Europe was flat or declining.
insights.locator: The US market is the most interesting

insights.claim: Virtually every shut US nuclear reactor that can feasibly be reopened is now somewhere in the restart process, after some had closed for being unprofitable.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Restart pipeline is the near-term nuclear supply lever; it is finite and largely already spoken for.
insights.quote: pretty much every shut nuclear reactor in the United States that feasibly can be reopened is now at various points in the restart process
insights.locator: We’ve also seen a few nuclear power plants

insights.claim: Small modular reactors are still very expensive, but their size and potential for factory construction offer big cost-saving potential; some produce high heat useful for chemical processes, and all are intrinsically safe, easing licensing and operation.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: SMR value hinges on achieving factory-scale serial production and industrial-heat applications.
insights.quote: Small modular reactors are still very expensive, but because they’re smaller and could plausibly be built in factories, they could have a big potential for significant cost savings.

insights.claim: Large-reactor construction in the US, UK, France and Europe suffers major cost overruns and delays because few plants are built and each differs from the last, so lessons and cost declines are not captured.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Western large-reactor projects carry high overrun risk until standardized fleet builds resume.
insights.quote: each plant is a little bit different from the last one, which makes it hard to lower costs when we are not building large numbers of the same thing
insights.locator: As for building more large plants

insights.claim: Korea and China build the same reactor designs repeatedly; at the UAE's four-unit Korean-designed Barakah plant the fourth unit came on much faster than the first, and repeatability is the No. 1 reason for lower cost and faster delivery.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: Standardized serial builds, not technology novelty, drive nuclear cost competitiveness.
insights.quote: Having a repeatable process is the No. 1 reason.

insights.claim: Serial reactor construction inside China at stunning scale has produced a vibrant Chinese nuclear industry, positioning China ahead of the West in nuclear build capability.
insights.speaker: Dimensional Fund Advisors
insights.so_what: China may dominate global nuclear supply chains and exports.
insights.quote: Inside China this is happening at a stunning scale, and it has produced a vibrant Chinese nuclear energy industry.
